It is Ordered, sentenced, and decreed, that there shall be yearly two General Assemblies or Courts, the one the second Thursday in April, the other the second Thursday in September following; the first shall be called the Court of Election, wherein shall be yearly chosen from time to time, so many Magistrates and other public Officers as shall be found requisite [needed]: Whereof one to be chosen Governor for the year ensuing and another be chosen, and no other Magistrate to be chosen for more than one year: provided always there be six chosen besides the Governor . . . which choice shall be made by all that are admitted freemen and have taken the Oath of Fidelity . . .

stimulus.image_alt: A grouped bar chart titled Population of the Virginia Colony, 1640-1710. For each of four years - 1640, 1680, 1700 and 1710 - a tall blue bar shows the total population of Virginia and a shorter orange bar shows the enslaved population. The total rises from roughly 10,000 in 1640 to about 80,000 in 1710. The enslaved population is near zero in 1640 and climbs to roughly 24,000 by 1710, growing faster than the total in the later years.

reps.exemplar: The colonial period establishes a founding civic principle — government by the consent of the governed — and extends it unevenly from the start. The principle traces to Magna Carta, where English barons forced King John to accept that the crown could not tax without the consent of a representative council (Doc 2). Colonists carried the same idea across the Atlantic: by 1639, Connecticut's Fundamental Orders had freemen electing their own governor and magistrates every year (Doc 1), and Virginia's House of Burgesses, seated in 1619 (outside information), had already extended the same principle even earlier. But consent of the governed consented for a shrinking circle of people even as the colonies grew. The same century that expanded self-rule for free male colonists brought epidemic disease that collapsed Native nations — one Massachusett population fell from thirty thousand to three hundred (Doc 3) — and built a labor system on enslavement: by 1710, roughly 24,000 of Virginia's 80,000 residents were enslaved, a share that had barely existed seventy years earlier (Doc 4). Virginia's slave codes of 1705 (outside information) locked that status in as permanent and inherited. The impact was a colonial society that could genuinely claim to be inventing self-government while denying it, by design, to most of the people living under it — a contradiction the Declaration of Independence would state out loud in 1776 without yet resolving.
reps.compare_focus: Name the civic principle explicitly (government by consent of the governed) AND add at least one accurate fact not in the documents (e.g., the House of Burgesses, 1619; Virginia's slave codes, 1705). Naming the principle is the 3→4 move.
compare_checklist: Did I name a civic/constitutional principle in plain words?
Did I add at least one accurate outside fact beyond the documents?
Did I connect the principle to the impact, not just list documents?
